challenges.name: dot-product-vs-cosine-quiz
challenges.title: Dot product or cosine?
challenges.description: Two pieces of vector-search code from the support assistant: which one lets vector length decide the ranking?

questions.explanation: True. score() is the dot product: 0.6*0.6 + 0.8*0.8 = 1.0 for kb-e1042, but 0.6*3.0 + 0.8*1.0 = 2.6 for the PDF page. The dot product is |q| * |v| * cos(angle), so the page wins only because its vector is long (|v| = 3.16). Its cosine is 2.6 / 3.16 = 0.82, below kb-e1042's 1.0. The misconception: a higher dot product means a more similar text. That holds only when every vector has the same length.

questions.question:
# ingest.py - every chunk vector is normalized once, when it is stored
vector = embed(chunk.text)
length = math.hypot(*vector)
index.add(chunk.id, [x / length for x in vector])

# search.py - the query vector is normalized the same way
score = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(query_vector, chunk_vector))

Statement: "search.py ranks chunks differently from cosine similarity, so it must also divide by both vector lengths at query time."
questions.explanation: False. Both vectors already have length 1, so |q| * |v| = 1 and the dot product equals the cosine: same scores, same ranking. Normalizing once at write time and using the cheaper dot product at query time is the usual design (it is what an inner-product index expects). The misconception: "dot product is always the bug". The bug is a dot product over vectors whose lengths differ - check the norms in the index, not the formula alone.

challenges.name: spot-the-ai-mistake-unnormalized-cosine
challenges.title: Spot the AI Mistake: cosine similarity without normalization
challenges.description: The support assistant's team sent this request to an AI assistant: "Write vector_search(query, chunks, top) for our support assistant. Rank the chunks by cosine similarity between their embedding and the query embedding and return the best `top` as {'id', 'score'}, with the score rounded to 4 decimals. Highest score first, ties by id. A chunk whose vector is all zeros has no direction: skip it. If the query vector is all zeros, return an empty list." The AI's code passed review and the public tests, which use the unit-length vectors of the embeddings API. Since the PDF import stores one vector per page (the sum of its paragraph vectors), "sync error E1042" returns the 4,000-word refund policy first, with a score of 4.92. Fix vector_search() so that it does what the request says: score = dot(query, vector) / (|query| * |vector|) rounded to 4 decimals, zero vectors skipped, an all-zero query returns [], sorted by score descending then id ascending, at most `top` results. All vectors in one call have the same dimension. The public tests pass on the AI's code; the hidden tests use vectors of different lengths.
hints: For two vectors that point in exactly the same direction, cosine similarity is 1.0 whatever their lengths. What does the AI's score give for [0.6, 0.8] against [0.6, 0.8], and against [3.0, 4.0]?
Look at the line that computes `score` and at the comment above it. Which part of the cosine formula is missing - and is it enough to fix only one of the two vectors?

A similar case on different numbers: for q = [1, 0] and v = [5, 5], the dot product is 5, |q| = 1 and |v| = math.hypot(5, 5) = 7.0711, so the cosine is 5 / (1 * 7.0711) = 0.7071. Scaling v to [50, 50] changes the dot product to 50 but leaves the cosine at 0.7071.
